dialog.body: Public Works, this is Lorraine, how can I help you this afternoon?
Yeah, hi, so it did it again. The corner. Same thing as last month, except worse this time, way worse.
Okay, I'm sorry, I'm going to need you to back up a little for me. Which corner are we talking about, and what happened?
The drain. The one my father called you guys about. On Wellington. We're at 9 Wellington Avenue, the [line breaks up] down at the end of the block.
You cut out on me there. I got 9 Wellington Avenue. Then I lost you.
Sorry, I'm in the car, the signal on this stretch is garbage. 9 Wellington. The storm drain on the corner. Our basement flooded again. That's twice now this winter. Twice.
Okay. 9 Wellington Avenue, basement flooded, and this is the second time this winter. Can I get your name?
Paulo Raposo. P-A-U-L-O. My father's Luis, it's his house, he's the one who called back in January.

Paulo Raposo, okay. Give me one second, let me pull up the address. [pause] Alright, I've got it. I see a call from Luis Raposo on January twenty-sixth, a drain backup at the corner, and it looks like a crew went out on the twenty-seventh.

Right, and you know what they did? They pulled the leaves off the top of the grate. That's it. Scraped the top off and drove away. Nobody looked underneath, nobody looked at the pipe, nothing. And now look.
So the crew cleared the grate on the twenty-seventh, and you're saying nothing was done below it.

Nothing. And my father told them, the whole block drains toward that corner. Everything, the whole street, it all runs down to that one grate. And the grate looks plugged again right now, I drove past it this morning, there's water just sitting on top of it.
Okay, I'm writing that down. Whole block drains to the corner, grate appears plugged as of this morning. When did the water come in this time?
Saturday night into Sunday. The nor'easter. Overnight. My father went down Sunday morning and it was about eight inches. Eight inches. The first time was like three.
About eight inches, overnight Saturday into Sunday, the twenty-second. And how's it getting in, is it coming up through the floor or...

No, same as last time. The basement windows, and the window well on the street side, the glass. Same exact spots. It fills up the well out front and comes right through. Nothing new, it's the same places, it's just more water because the street's got nowhere to go.
Same entry points as January, the basement windows and the window well glass on the street side. Got it.
[crosstalk] hang on, hang on, sorry. I got my granddaughter here on speaker with me, she's in the car seat. She thinks this is funny.
Oh, that's alright.
She's giggling at the phone, she likes your voice, I don't know. Okay. Sorry. Where was I.
You were telling me how the water got in. Was there any damage to things down there?

Same stuff as the first time, honestly. The paint cans, the ladders, my father's workbench and all his hand tools. All of it wet again. Nothing new got hit, it's the same corner of the basement, but that's not the point. The point is we already paid to have that whole basement cleaned out and dried once. We paid for that. In January. And now we're doing it all over again because nobody fixed the drain.
I understand. So you had it professionally cleaned and dried after the first flood, and now the same items, the paint cans, ladders, workbench and hand tools, got wet again.

Yeah. And I'm not trying to yell at you, I know you're just answering the phone. But I don't want another guy with a rake. I want somebody who actually knows what's under that street to come look at it. A supervisor, an engineer, somebody. Because clearing the top didn't do anything. You can see it didn't do anything.

Okay. So what I can do is log this as a repeat backup, since it's the same location as the January call, and I'll put in that the previous visit only cleared the grate. That way whoever goes out knows this isn't a first visit and they need to look at the line, not just the top.
When, though? Because there's [inaudible] coming, I saw something about more rain.
I missed part of that. You said more rain coming?
Yeah, they're saying more later in the week maybe. When's somebody coming?

The crews have been all over the place since Sunday, but I can get you on for Wednesday, the twenty-fifth. And separate from that I'm requesting a supervisor call you back, by Thursday the twenty-sixth at the latest, about looking at it more seriously.
Wednesday crew and a supervisor calls by Thursday.
That's right. Wednesday the twenty-fifth for the crew, supervisor callback by Thursday the twenty-sixth. Who should the supervisor call, you or your father?
Me. Call me. My father, he gets worked up, and I'm the one who's gonna push on this. My cell is 401-555-0164.
Yeah. And put in there that it's twice. Because last time it was like, oh, big storm, it happens. Twice in a month is not it happens. Something's wrong with that drain.

I've got it in the notes. Second flood at this address this winter, first on January twenty-sixth at about three inches, second overnight February twenty-first into the twenty-second at about eight inches, same entry points both times, whole block drains to the corner, grate looked plugged this morning, and the caller is requesting a supervisor or engineer look at the drain itself and not just the grate.
Okay. Yeah. That's it. That's everything.
And if it backs up again before Wednesday, if you see water pooling at that corner, call us back right away and reference this, and we'll try to get somebody there sooner.
If it backs up before Wednesday the basement's already underwater, that's the whole problem. [pause] Sorry. She's laughing again. Okay, okay, we're almost done, baby.
That's alright. Is there anything else I can put on the report for you?
No. Just, please, have somebody actually look at it this time. Not just the top. We can't keep paying to dry that thing out.
I hear you. It's flagged as a repeat, and the supervisor will be calling you on your cell. You get home safe with your granddaughter, okay?
Yeah. Thanks. Wednesday. I'm gonna be watching for them.
